name: Closed Interrogative Clause
pattern: Clause: (Subject:XP +) Head:VP[closed interrogative; main-clause subject–auxiliary inversion]

entry.name: Closed Interrogative Clause
entry.pattern: Clause: (Subject:XP +) Head:VP[closed interrogative; main-clause subject–auxiliary inversion]

dimensions.form: Clause headed by a VP; main clauses show clause-type-triggered subject–auxiliary inversion, while subordinate content clauses are normally marked by whether or if and retain basic Subject–Predicator order
dimensions.meaning: Characteristically presents a closed set of answers, prototypically the positive and negative values of a proposition
dimensions.function: Characteristically asks a closed question, but can perform directives, acknowledgements, statements, and other indirect speech acts
dimensions.distribution: Tensed main clauses and subordinate closed-interrogative content clauses

1.definition: A headed clause type characteristically used to present a closed question
1.details: Closed and open interrogatives are distinct primary clause types in CGEL, not syntactic subtypes defined by a shared interrogative form. In main closed interrogatives, clause type itself triggers subject–auxiliary inversion and do-support where no other auxiliary is available. Subordinate closed interrogatives normally use whether or if without inversion. Closed-question force is characteristic rather than necessary: Would you mind opening the door? is syntactically closed interrogative but conventionally functions as a directive (CGEL pp. 853–57, 865–72, 951–55).

examples.note: Main closed interrogative with subject–auxiliary inversion
Do-support supplies the auxiliary required by main-clause inversion

examples.form: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].
examples.note: Subordinate closed interrogative with whether and basic Subject–Predicator order
Closed interrogative conventionally used as an indirect directive

constraints.description: The construction remains a Clause headed by VP. In a main clause the finite auxiliary precedes the Subject through subject–auxiliary inversion; subordinate closed interrogatives normally have whether/if marking and no inversion.
The characteristic question defines a closed answer set; alternative questions are a use of coordination with closed-interrogative syntax, not a sixth clause type.
Inquiry force is not necessary: indirect directives and strongly biased or rhetorical uses retain closed-interrogative clause type.

projection.target: Clause-type-triggered inversion in a main clause, or subordinate whether/if marking, predicts a closed answer space and the corresponding main/subordinate distribution, while leaving room for indirect forces such as directives
projection.evidence: The inversion and subordinator diagnostics distinguish closed interrogatives from declaratives and open interrogatives independently of whether a particular utterance is used to inquire

grounds.note: Main inversion and subordinate whether/if marking project answer-space and distributional contrasts
The linked main/subordinate profile recurs independently of actual inquiry force

diagnostics: basic Subject–Predicator order in the standard variety

relatedConstructions.notes: Closed and open interrogatives are distinct primary clause types with different syntactic marking
A declarative question asks without subject–auxiliary inversion and carries a stronger same-polarity bias

grounds.note: Closed-interrogative syntax, closed questions, indirect-force uses, and main/subordinate contrast

curious.title: Questions with a fixed set of answers
curious.summary: Some clauses are built to ask a question with a closed set of answers, such as yes or no.
curious.body:
Are you generous? and Did Kim finish the report? are built to ask a closed question, one with a fixed set of possible answers, such as yes or no. In these, the helping word (are, did) comes before the person.

Inside a longer sentence the pattern changes. In I wonder whether Kim finished the report, the question is tucked into the sentence, introduced by whether, and the words keep their ordinary order.

The form doesn't force the use. Would you mind opening the door? has the same build but works as a polite request.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

curious.try: Take a statement, such as You are hungry. How do you turn it into a question with a yes or no answer?

teacher.summary: Covers yes/no questions in main and subordinate clauses, including do-support and indirect uses such as requests.
teacher.explain: A closed interrogative is a Clause that characteristically asks a closed question: the answers are a closed set, prototypically positive or negative. In a main clause the clause type triggers subject-auxiliary inversion, and do-support supplies an auxiliary when none is present (Did Kim finish the report?). A subordinate closed interrogative normally uses whether or if with ordinary subject-verb order. Closed-question force is characteristic, not necessary: Would you mind opening the door? is a closed interrogative that conventionally works as a directive.
teacher.terms: Yes/no question or polar question are sometimes-used labels for the positive-or-negative cases, and are narrower than closed interrogative, which also covers alternative questions. Open interrogatives (wh-questions) are a separate clause type.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

contrasts.note: Closed interrogative. Do-support supplies the auxiliary that comes before the subject.

watch_for: A learner might read Would you mind opening the door? as only asking about willingness, when it is conventionally a request.
A learner might look for an auxiliary in Did Kim finish the report? and miss that do supplies one.
A learner might carry main-clause inversion into the subordinate clause after wonder.
teacher.activity: Students turn statements into closed questions (You are hungry, Kim finished the report) and then tuck each into I wonder whether. They say what changed in word order between the two versions.

child.hook: Which questions can you answer with yes or no?
child.explain: Some questions have a short set of answers, like yes or no. In Are you generous? the helping word are comes before the person. In Did Kim finish the report? the helping word did is added to make the question.
child.play: Turn You are hungry into a question. Which word moves in front of the person? Then turn Kim finished the report into a question. Which helping word gets added?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms now say yes/no and polar question are narrower labels than closed interrogative (which also covers alternative questions); child explanation and game now say did is added by do-support rather than moved.
